idiom_name: NSCondition lock/wait/signal/broadcast with the documented predicate loop
implementation_notes: Foundation's NSCondition is a POSIX-style condition variable that carries its own lock, and Apple's documentation spells out the protocol: lock, test the predicate, wait while it is false, retest after every return, do the work, signal if the task changed state, unlock - with the explicit warning that signals can be spurious, which is why the predicate is mandatory. DispatchSemaphore from Dispatch is the lighter alternative when the guard is simply 'a permit is available'. Use NSCondition for thread-based libraries; for anything that can be asynchronous, express the same guard with Swift concurrency (AsyncStream or an actor) so no thread is parked.
pitfalls: NSCondition.wait() returns for spurious reasons: the while loop is the contract, not an optimisation.
Mixing NSCondition with Swift concurrency blocks a cooperative-pool thread, so a guard reached from async code should be an AsyncStream or an actor instead.
Every lock needs an unlock on every path; a thrown error between lock and unlock leaves the condition permanently locked.

variants.name: Swift concurrency: AsyncStream / for-await
variants.implementation_notes: Swift concurrency expresses the suspension as an await instead of a park: AsyncStream is built from a continuation, the producer yields elements and finishes the stream, and `for await` suspends the task until the next element arrives - Apple documents exactly this adaptation of callback- or delegation-based APIs to async-await, which covers the common guard 'an item is available' without a condition variable. Choose it when the waiting code is already async, and set a buffering policy because the default buffer is unbounded.
pitfalls: The default buffering policy is unbounded (Int.max), so a fast producer grows memory until a bounded policy or backpressure is set.
A stream that is never finished leaves for-await suspended forever, and yield after finish is silently dropped.
